title: Section 14 Limitation Act — Wrong forum in good faith

content.overview: Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963 excludes time spent prosecuting another civil proceeding that fails for want of jurisdiction or another cause of a like nature. For a suit, the plaintiff must have prosecuted with due diligence another civil proceeding against the same defendant, on the same matter in issue, in good faith, in a court which from defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature could not entertain it. Section 14(2) makes the same exclusion for an application. The exclusion is of that prosecution time. It is not a general condonation, and it does not apply to a forum that could have entertained the matter.
content.study: Require the same matter, due diligence, good faith, and a court that could not entertain the proceeding. A merits dismissal is not a section 14 defect. Do not use section 14 to save a late filing that was never prosecuted in another court.

learningObjectives: State the section 14 conditions for a suit and an application.
Require defect of jurisdiction or a like cause.
Keep a merits failure outside the section.
enhancement.definition: Section 14 excludes time spent diligently and in good faith on the same matter in a court that could not entertain it, when computing limitation for the later suit or application.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The later court does not add a new period. It leaves out time lost to a proceeding the earlier court could not hear.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Limitation Act, 1963, section 14. Section 5 is condonation. Section 14 is exclusion.
essentialIngredients: Defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature
Earlier court unable to entertain it
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 14(1) is the suit rule. The excluded time is the time during which the plaintiff has been prosecuting the other civil proceeding. That proceeding may be in a court of first instance or in appeal or revision. It must be against the defendant, relate to the same matter in issue, and be prosecuted in good faith in a court which, from defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature, is unable to entertain it. Section 14(2) applies the exclusion to an application, with the defendant in the later application corresponding to the opposite party. Section 14(3) excludes a period already excluded under section 9 of the old Act in the stated way; ordinary problems do not need it. A dismissal on the merits is not inability to entertain. A voluntary withdrawal from a court that had jurisdiction is not this section.
examples: A title suit is filed in a court which lacks territorial jurisdiction and is returned. The time of that prosecution is excluded in the later suit if diligence and good faith are shown.
The first court had jurisdiction and dismissed the suit on evidence. Section 14 does not exclude that time.
No earlier proceeding was filed. Section 14 has nothing to exclude.
enhancement.problemApplication: List forum, dates, same parties, same matter, diligence, good faith, and why the first court could not entertain the case. If the first court could decide it, refuse the exclusion.
distinctions: Want of jurisdiction vs dismissal on merits
Same matter vs a new claim
Prosecuted time vs idle time before filing
